title: Separate the Currier ed preference from a one-way chronology claim
statement: Timm (2014, v3), section 9, graphs 11–12 and pp. 24–25, uses od/ed pairs to motivate the proposal that Currier B followed A (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1407.6639v3). I counted exact forms among certain paragraph tokens on public practice training pages in ZL3b, IT2a and RF1b. In ZL3b (9,333 A and 19,711 B tokens), the A/B counts for chedy were 1/405, chedar 0/30, chedal 0/21 and qokeedy 0/279. In ZL3b, chodal itself was 0/4. IT2a and RF1b also each gave two A instances of chedy. I enumerated exact alternatives made by replacing one written EVA od with ed, holding all other characters fixed. For exclusivity I required at least two instances on one side, zero on the other, and at least one instance of the paired form on each side. ZL3b had 52 B-only ed pairs and one A-only od pair. The reverse example cthody/cthedy held in all three transliterations: ZL3b cthody 11/0 and cthedy 1/11, IT2a 13/0 and 1/8, RF1b 10/0 and 1/9. In 100 uniform draws without replacement of 9,333 selected ZL3b tokens per side (seed 503), the median counts were 31 B-only ed pairs and one A-only od pair. Restricting ZL3b to section H and matching 3,151 tokens per side gave medians of 14 B-only ed pairs and zero A-only od pairs. These checks reproduce an asymmetric spelling preference under this grouping and qualify the strict one-way generalization. Token matching can turn a rare form into a sample zero. Spelling preferences alone leave the chronological direction open.
check: Reproduce the counts using the public practice training pages, EVA ZL3b, IT2a, RF1b, Currier A/B and certain paragraph words only. Repeat the stated single-site od-to-ed pairing with the same seeds and report page-level or scribal sensitivity. To test chronological ordering, require an independent direction indicator from physical or scribal evidence and report whether the linguistic comparison predicts it.
